title: Apartheid South Africa and protest (1948–1964)
summary: How the National Party built apartheid after 1948, how the ANC and others protested non-violently, and how Sharpeville led to bans, armed struggle and the Rivonia Trial.

keyterms.definition: 'Separateness': the National Party's system of legalised racial segregation and white minority rule from 1948.
1950 law classifying every South African by race, the foundation of apartheid.
1950 law assigning residential and business areas to racial groups, leading to forced removals such as Sophiatown.
Laws forcing Black Africans to carry passes (reference books from 1952) controlling where they could live and work.
1953 law placing Black schooling under state control with an inferior curriculum to prepare pupils for manual labour.
1952 ANC-led mass civil disobedience in which volunteers deliberately broke apartheid laws; over 8,000 were arrested.
Statement of principles adopted at the Congress of the People, Kliptown, June 1955, declaring South Africa belongs to all who live in it.
Pan Africanist Congress, an Africanist breakaway from the ANC founded in 1959 under Robert Sobukwe.
21 March 1960: police fired on a PAC anti-pass protest, killing 69 people.
'Spear of the Nation': armed wing formed by ANC and Communist Party members in 1961 to carry out sabotage.
1963–64 trial of MK leaders, including Mandela, ending in life sentences in June 1964.
Minister of Native Affairs (1950–58) and Prime Minister (1958–66), chief architect of 'grand apartheid' and the homelands.

questions.prompt: Which party won the 1948 election and introduced apartheid?
questions.explanation: D.F. Malan's National Party won with support from Afrikaner voters fearful of Black urbanisation.

questions.prompt: Match each law to what it did.

pairs.right: State control of inferior Black schooling

questions.explanation: Together these laws (1949–53) built 'petty' and 'grand' apartheid.

questions.text: The ANC's 1952 campaign of deliberate law-breaking was called the ___ Campaign.
questions.explanation: It boosted ANC membership dramatically; the state responded with harsher penalties for protest.

questions.statement: The Freedom Charter of 1955 called for a South Africa belonging to all who live in it, Black and white.
questions.explanation: Its non-racial vision later caused Africanists to break away and form the PAC in 1959.

questions.prompt: What was the outcome of the Treason Trial (1956–1961)?
options: All the accused were eventually acquitted
It was moved to the UN
questions.explanation: 156 activists were charged; all were acquitted by 1961, but the trial tied up leaders for years.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.
items: Congress of the People adopts the Freedom Charter
Women's march to the Union Buildings

questions.prompt: What did about 20,000 women protest against at the Union Buildings in Pretoria on 9 August 1956?
options: Extension of pass laws to women
questions.explanation: The march, organised by the Federation of South African Women, is commemorated as Women's Day in South Africa.

questions.text: The architect of 'grand apartheid', ___, became prime minister in 1958.
questions.explanation: Verwoerd's Promotion of Bantu Self-Government Act (1959) laid the basis for separate 'homelands'.

questions.statement: Sophiatown in Johannesburg was destroyed and its residents forcibly removed under apartheid legislation from 1955.
questions.explanation: Its mixed community was moved to Meadowlands (Soweto) and a white suburb, Triomf, was built on the site.

questions.prompt: Why did the PAC break away from the ANC in 1959?
options: It rejected the ANC's multiracial alliances and wanted an Africanist approach
It wanted to cooperate with the National Party
questions.explanation: Sobukwe and others objected to the ANC's ties with white and Indian Congress allies and the Communist Party.

questions.prompt: Which organisation called the anti-pass protest at Sharpeville on 21 March 1960?
questions.explanation: The PAC launched its campaign ten days before an ANC anti-pass campaign was due to start.
Many were shot in the back while fleeing; the massacre drew international condemnation.

questions.statement: After Sharpeville the government declared a state of emergency and banned the ANC and PAC.
questions.explanation: The Unlawful Organisations Act (April 1960) forced both movements underground and into exile.

questions.prompt: Why did ANC leaders turn to sabotage in 1961?
options: They believed non-violent protest had been met with violence and banning, leaving no peaceful channel
They had won power in elections
The PAC had already defeated the state
questions.explanation: MK targeted installations rather than people at first, launching attacks on 16 December 1961.

questions.prompt: Match each person to their role.

pairs.right: ANC president awarded the Nobel Peace Prize

questions.explanation: Luthuli received the 1960 Nobel Peace Prize, presented in December 1961.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.
questions.explanation: March 1960, May 1961, December 1961, July 1963, June 1964.

questions.prompt: What did the General Laws Amendment Act of 1963 allow?
options: Detention without trial for up to 90 days
questions.explanation: The 90-day law allowed repeated detention and was used against activists, often with torture.

questions.text: Mandela and other Rivonia defendants were imprisoned on ___ Island.
questions.explanation: Mandela spent 18 of his 27 years in prison on Robben Island.

questions.statement: By 1964 the internal resistance movement had been severely weakened by arrests, bans and exile.
questions.explanation: Mass resistance revived only in the 1970s with Black Consciousness and the 1976 Soweto uprising.

questions.prompt: Which international response to apartheid occurred by 1964?
options: South Africa was excluded from the Tokyo Olympics
The UN imposed a mandatory arms embargo
The USA broke off diplomatic relations
questions.explanation: The 1963 UN Security Council arms embargo was voluntary (mandatory only in 1977); Western trade continued.
